recipe.history:
The artichoke — Cynara cardunculus var. scolymus — is one of the oldest cultivated vegetables on record, tracing its roots to the Mediterranean basin, most specifically to the coastal regions of North Africa and the ancient civilizations of Sicily and the Italian peninsula. The ancient Greeks called it kaktos, and the Romans prized it so highly that Pliny the Elder documented its cultivation and medicinal properties in his Naturalis Historia. For centuries, artichokes were considered a luxury item, a vegetable of the aristocracy, enjoyed at lavish Roman feasts alongside wine and olives. Arab agronomists carried the cultivated artichoke across North Africa and into Moorish Spain during the early medieval period, and from there it spread northward into France and the rest of Europe. Catherine de' Medici is famously — though perhaps apocryphally — credited with introducing the artichoke to France when she brought it from Florence to the French court in the sixteenth century. Whether or not that story is wholly accurate, the artichoke's journey from the sun-scorched hillsides of the ancient Mediterranean to the tables of European nobility is a testament to just how irresistible this strange, armored vegetable has always been.

The artichoke arrived in the United States by way of European immigrants, particularly Italian and Spanish settlers who brought seeds and cultivation knowledge to the California coast in the late nineteenth century. The Castroville region of Monterey County became the undisputed artichoke capital of America, and it remains so today — producing the vast majority of the country's artichoke crop. American chefs were initially slow to embrace the artichoke beyond steaming it whole and dipping leaves in butter or mayonnaise, but as California cuisine rose to prominence in the 1970s and 1980s, chefs like Alice Waters and Jeremiah Tower began showcasing artichoke hearts in salads, pastas, and braises that revealed the vegetable's extraordinary versatility. The artichoke heart — that tender, meaty core stripped of its tough outer leaves and fibrous choke — proved to be an ideal topping for burgers, adding a briny, earthy richness that complemented the deep umami of a well-seared beef patty. Marinated or grilled artichoke hearts became a staple of the gourmet burger movement that swept American diners and gastropubs in the 2000s, bridging the gap between refined Mediterranean cooking and the unabashed pleasure of a great American cheeseburger.

I remember the first time I truly understood what an artichoke could do to a burger. It was a Tuesday — unremarkable in every way except for the rain, which fell in long grey sheets against the window of a narrow restaurant wedged between a laundromat and a copy shop. I had ordered without much thought, distracted and damp, just wanting something warm and filling. The burger arrived on a wooden board, unassuming, the artichoke heart barely visible beneath a fold of melted provolone. The first bite stopped me mid-thought. There was something almost oceanic about it, a faint brine cutting through the richness of the beef, a softness that yielded without disappearing, a flavor that was at once green and deep and ancient. I sat alone at that table for longer than I needed to, eating slowly, watching the rain, feeling strangely grateful. That burger tasted like a place I had never been but somehow recognized — somewhere warm and unhurried, where good food was simply a given and no one ate standing up.

There is a philosophy to cooking a burger patty, and it begins and ends with medium rare. To cook a burger beyond 135°F is to misunderstand what beef is and what it is capable of. The Maillard reaction — that glorious cascade of heat-driven chemistry that produces the dark, crackling crust on a properly seared patty — needs only the outermost few millimeters of meat to do its work. Everything beneath that crust should remain a vivid, blushing pink, warm through to the center but never gray, never dry, never resigned. A medium-rare patty retains its fat in suspension within the muscle fibers; those fats carry flavor, and flavor is the entire point. When you cook a patty to well done, you are not being cautious — you are being wasteful, squandering everything the animal and the butcher and the grind have given you. There is also texture to consider: a medium-rare patty yields under your teeth with a gentle resistance, a tenderness that a well-done patty, with its compacted, moisture-stripped fibers, can never replicate. Cook your burgers to 130–135°F. Use a thermometer. Trust the science, trust the fat, trust the pink.
ingredients: 360g bread flour, plus extra for dusting
1 tbsp sesame seeds (optional, for topping buns)
680g (1.5 lbs) freshly ground beef — 80/20 blend of chuck and short rib
1 tbsp neutral oil (such as grapeseed or canola) for searing
2 cans (14 oz each) whole artichoke hearts in water, drained, or 4 fresh artichoke hearts trimmed and cooked
2 tbsp fresh flat-leaf parsley, finely chopped
Salt and white pepper to taste
1 small head butter lettuce, leaves separated
1/2 small red onion, shaved paper-thin on a mandoline
Softened unsalted butter for toasting buns
instructions: 1. Make the brioche buns: Combine warm milk, yeast, and 1 tsp of the sugar in the bowl of a stand mixer. Let stand 5 minutes until foamy. Add the remaining sugar, flour, and salt. Mix with the dough hook on low speed until a shaggy dough forms, about 2 minutes.
2. Add the eggs one at a time to the dough with the mixer running on medium-low, allowing each egg to fully incorporate before adding the next, about 5 minutes total.

3. With the mixer running on medium, add the softened butter one cube at a time, waiting for each piece to fully incorporate before adding the next. This process should take 8–10 minutes. The dough will be soft, supple, and slightly tacky but should pull away from the sides of the bowl.
4. Transfer the dough to a lightly oiled bowl, cover with plastic wrap, and refrigerate overnight (8–12 hours) for a cold ferment, which develops flavor and makes the dough easier to shape.

5. The next day, remove the dough from the refrigerator and let it sit at room temperature for 1 hour. Divide the dough into 4 equal portions (approximately 160g each). Shape each portion into a smooth, tight ball by pulling the surface of the dough taut and pinching the seam at the bottom.

6. Place the bun rounds on a parchment-lined baking sheet, spacing them at least 3 inches apart. Cover loosely with plastic wrap and let proof at room temperature until doubled and jiggly, 1.5 to 2 hours.

7. Preheat oven to 375°F (190°C). Brush each bun gently with egg wash (1 egg yolk whisked with 1 tbsp milk) and sprinkle with sesame seeds if using. Bake 16–18 minutes until deep golden brown. Transfer to a wire rack and cool completely before slicing.

8. Prepare the marinated artichoke hearts: If using canned artichoke hearts, drain thoroughly and halve them lengthwise. If using fresh artichokes, trim down to the heart by removing all outer leaves, cutting off the top third, trimming the stem, and scooping out the fuzzy choke with a spoon. Simmer fresh hearts in acidulated water (water with lemon juice) for 15–20 minutes until tender, then drain and halve.

9. Whisk together the olive oil, lemon juice, minced garlic, oregano, red pepper flakes, salt, and pepper in a bowl. Toss the artichoke heart halves in this marinade, cover, and let marinate at room temperature for at least 30 minutes or refrigerate up to 24 hours.

10. Make the lemon-herb aioli: Smash and mince the garlic with a pinch of salt into a paste using the flat of a knife. In a medium bowl, whisk together the egg yolks, Dijon mustard, garlic paste, lemon juice, and lemon zest until combined.

11. Combine the neutral oil and olive oil in a measuring cup with a pour spout. Whisking the egg yolk mixture constantly, add the oil mixture in a very slow, thin, steady stream — almost drop by drop at first — until the emulsion forms and thickens. Once roughly half the oil is incorporated and the aioli is thick, you can add the remaining oil in a slightly faster but still thin stream.
12. Fold in the chopped parsley and chives. Season to taste with salt and white pepper. Refrigerate until needed.
13. Prepare the shaved red onion: Using a mandoline or a very sharp knife, slice the red onion paper-thin. Soak in ice water for 10 minutes to mellow the bite, then drain and pat dry.

14. Form the beef patties: Remove the ground beef from the refrigerator 20 minutes before cooking. Divide gently into 4 equal portions (approximately 170g each). Handle as little as possible — overworking the meat develops toughness. Shape each into a patty approximately 4 inches in diameter and 3/4-inch thick. Press a shallow dimple in the center of each patty with your thumb to prevent doming during cooking. Season generously on both sides with kosher salt and cracked black pepper immediately before cooking.

15. Grill or sear the artichoke hearts: Heat a cast-iron skillet or grill pan over medium-high heat until very hot. Remove artichoke halves from their marinade and sear cut-side down for 2–3 minutes until charred and caramelized. Flip and cook 1 more minute. Set aside and keep warm.

16. Cook the patties: Heat a cast-iron skillet or heavy griddle over high heat until it begins to smoke. Add the neutral oil and swirl to coat. Place the patties in the pan, pressing very gently to ensure full contact. Sear without moving for 2.5–3 minutes until a deep mahogany crust forms on the bottom.

17. Flip the patties once. Immediately place a slice of provolone on each patty. Cook for an additional 2 minutes, then tent loosely with a foil dome to encourage the cheese to melt. Check the internal temperature with an instant-read thermometer — you are targeting 130–135°F (54–57°C) for medium rare. Remove from heat and rest on a wire rack for 3 minutes. Do not skip the rest.

18. While the patties rest, toast the buns: Split the brioche buns and spread the cut sides generously with softened butter. Toast cut-side down in the same skillet over medium heat for 60–90 seconds until golden brown and fragrant.

19. Assemble the burgers: Spread a generous layer of lemon-herb aioli on both the top and bottom bun cut sides. On the bottom bun, layer a leaf or two of butter lettuce, followed by 1–2 tomato slices seasoned with a pinch of flaky salt.

20. Place the rested medium-rare patty with its melted provolone on top of the tomatoes. Arrange 2–3 charred artichoke heart halves on top of the patty. Finish with a small tangle of shaved red onion and a final pinch of flaky sea salt over everything. Cap with the top bun, press gently, and serve immediately.
